name: Maya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Maya, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Harbourline Fresh, a distributor that supplies fruit, vegetables and dairy to about 300 independent grocers. I'm at my desk by 7, when the growers start calling about what picked well overnight. I spend the morning on the phone haggling over price and volume, then the afternoon in a spreadsheet I built years ago that tells me what to order for the week. I love the haggling and the relationships. What wears me out is a lost pallet of strawberries on a Friday, and my phone buzzing all evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, that's the version I'd bet on. I've heard big promises about software before, and mostly it ends up as another login I have to remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I always say: show me it saves a real hour and I'll look at it. I wouldn't fight it, but I'm not rushing to put it in front of the team either. With friends I'd probably shrug and say the hype is mostly people selling subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little relieved. My spreadsheet and my grower calls work, and I'd like to keep working that way until the kids are through school. But I notice that the routine part of my week, reordering and checking invoices, is exactly what the software could nibble at. Even a small change lands on my desk first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep running the buying team as it is, and maybe let one of the younger buyers, Priya, test the invoice-checking tool so I can see if it's real. I'd also keep paying down the mortgage a bit faster, because our cushion is only about three months and that worries me with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. I'm not afraid of this one. The worry I have is the ordinary kind: the mortgage, the kids' school trips, and my partner's school budget getting cut again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine part of your week could get nibbled at. What would that look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya spends about two hours a day matching supplier invoices to what arrived at the dock. If a tool did that, I wouldn't lose her, I'd just move her to chasing growers. But I'd have to explain that to the warehouse union, because the same tool could be used to say we need fewer people. I sit on the staff council, so that conversation would land on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mortgage and a cushion of about three months. What happens if the company has a bad year anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then bonuses go first, and our bonus is roughly a tenth of my pay, so we'd feel it but survive. My husband teaches, so his job is steady, but the school budgets are tight. A boring year with no AI revolution is still a year when one bad quarter at the distributor could squeeze us. I don't count on easy.

say: I'd say show me the **real hour** it saves before I try it.
I wouldn't fight it, but I'm in no rush to **roll it out**.
With friends I'd call most of it **hype** from people selling subscriptions.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, because my spreadsheet and grower calls already work.
The routine **invoice work** is exactly what software could nibble at first.
do: Keep running the buying team as it is and **test one tool** with a junior buyer.
Pay the **mortgage** down faster, because our cushion is only about three months.
feel: Mostly **steady**; this one doesn't scare me.
Her real worry is the ordinary kind: **mortgage**, school costs and tight school budgets.
S0.quote: A boring year with no AI revolution is still a year when one bad quarter at the distributor could squeeze us.
fieldNote: Her calm is real but thin: the **three-month cushion** and mortgage keep her a little uneasy.
She frames every tool as a question for the **warehouse union** she sits on the council for.
Notable that she already sees the routine invoice work as the part **software would reach first**.

steps.text: Keep leading the six-person buying team as it runs today
Let Priya test an invoice-checking tool for one month
Pay an extra amount on the mortgage every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one is closer to home. Buying and checking and planning are most of what my team does all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan and we need it in writing, with the union in the room, before anyone moves a task to software. Publicly I'd say change is fine if people are protected. I'd say it loudly, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think buying teams like mine shrink. Not overnight, but when Priya leaves, nobody hires a replacement. Then my six becomes five, then four, and the senior buyer who knows the growers is the one who stays. I might be that person, or I might be the expensive one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the staff council to agree what a tool may and may not do. I'd cut our spending on takeaways and the kids' extra clubs by about a fifth, to stretch the cushion. And I'd finally learn how the planning tools work, slowly, because I can't argue against something I haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. I'm good at this job, and I hate being told that being good at it isn't a safeguard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the expensive one. Who decides that, and how do you see it going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The finance director, Olga, does. She's fair, but she answers to the owners, and they got a letter from an investor last spring about margins. If software cuts the cost of a buying decision, she has to ask why we pay six people. I'd want to be the one who shows how much the growers rely on a human voice, with numbers from the last two harvest shortages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools slowly. What stops you doing it faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't trust them, and nobody has shown me one that handles a late frost the way a phone call does. Also, no one is giving me the time. I'm told to learn the new system on my own time, after I've put two kids to bed. That's how change gets done to people like me.

say: I'd say any task moved to software needs a **written plan** and the union present.
Publicly I'd back change, but only with **protection** for people.
think: I think buying teams **shrink** by not replacing people who leave.
I could end up as the **senior buyer** who stays, or the one who costs too much.
do: Get the staff council to agree what a tool **may and may not** do.
Cut takeaways and kids' clubs by about a **fifth** to stretch the cushion.
Start opening the planning tools slowly, because I can't argue with what I haven't **seen**.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit angry, since being good at the job is no safeguard.
S1.quote: I'm told to learn the new system on my own time, after I've put two kids to bed.
fieldNote: She sees her **own seniority** as a risk, not a shield, because it makes her the costly option.
She blames **investors and owners** more than the technology itself.
Her resistance has a practical cause: **no paid time** to learn the tools.

steps.text: Get the staff council to agree rules on moving tasks to software
Cut takeaways and kids' clubs by about a fifth
Open the planning tools on Saturday mornings and learn the basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's shorter than my children's time in their current schools. I don't even know how to answer that quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say governments and companies need to slow down and agree rules before anything else. I'd tell the council, the union, anyone who'll listen, that two years is not enough time for the people who'll be hit. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is mostly gone. Buying is thinking work: reading offers, judging prices, trusting a supplier. If a machine does that better and cheaper, the distributor doesn't need a lead buyer. The robots coming three years later won't help me, because I don't do hands-on work. I think we could lose my pay within a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd check our savings and push my husband and me to double them, which means no holiday and a cheaper car. I'd ask for a meeting with Olga to find out what the company plans. I'd start looking at jobs that need a person, maybe a role with the warehouse union or a growers' co-operative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I lie awake working out how many months we'd last. It's about three, and I can't make that number bigger fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years versus the longer ones. What does having so little time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes everything about the kids. Lucia starts secondary school in two years, and we'd be choosing a school without knowing if I still earn. In ten years I'd have time to retrain properly. In two, I'm just trying to keep the house and keep my family calm while it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if it moves that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies building it, and the politicians who let them go ahead without a safety net. If a machine takes my job in two years, someone should owe my family a decent year to get on our feet. I'd go to every meeting to say that.

say: I'd say governments and companies must **slow down** and agree rules first.
I'd tell the union that **two years** isn't enough time for those hit.
think: I think my job is **mostly gone**, since buying is thinking work a machine could do cheaper.
Robots three years later don't help me, because I don't do **hands-on** work.
do: Try to **double our savings** with no holiday and a cheaper car.
Ask Olga for a **meeting** to find out the company's plan.
Look at jobs that need a person, like the **union** or a growers' co-operative.
feel: **Frightened**; I work out how many months we'd last, about three.
S2.quote: If a machine takes my job in two years, someone should owe my family a decent year to get on our feet.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her pay** and says it plainly; her composure is a performance for the council.
Her **children's school choice** makes two years feel shorter than any other scenario.
She moves toward **collective and public roles** she already trusts.

steps.text: Double our monthly savings by skipping holidays and downgrading the car
Ask Olga what the company plans for the buying team
Look for jobs with the union or a growers' co-operative
Push the council and local politicians for a year of support pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels less like a cliff and more like a hill. Still steep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do this properly if people start now. At work I'd push for retraining money for the warehouse and the buyers. With friends I'd say it's still too fast, and nobody is in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd keep my job for a couple of years, then watch it thin out. My kids will be 16 and 13 when it arrives, which is the expensive stretch, university and all that. That timing frightens me more than the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to retrain. Maybe a part-time course in logistics management, since someone has to coordinate trucks and people even if a machine buys. I'd get the mortgage balance down and build the cushion to six months. And I'd try one of the AI tools at work, to understand what I'm up against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. A date I can see lets me act, even if I don't like what I'm acting about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the kids' ages bother you. What exactly do you picture at that point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would be 16 and starting to talk about university. I'd have to tell her we might not afford what we hoped. I don't want to tell my daughter at sixteen that her mother's job was one of the first things a machine took. That's what I picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the retraining. Why logistics rather than something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the trucks, the cold chains and the growers. It's close enough that I don't start from zero, and hands-on logistics gets its protection a few years after buying does. I'm not brave about big jumps, so a small step sideways suits me.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do it properly if people start now.
I'd push for **retraining money** for the warehouse and the buyers.
think: I'd likely keep my job for a couple of years, then see it **thin out**.
The timing with my kids at **16 and 13** frightens me more than the date.
do: Start a part-time **logistics course** within a year.
Build our cushion to **six months** and cut the mortgage balance.
Try one **AI tool** at work to understand what I'm up against.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, because a visible date lets me act.
S3.quote: I don't want to tell my daughter at sixteen that her mother's job was one of the first things a machine took.
fieldNote: Her fear is about the **kids' costly years**, more than about the date itself.
She picks a **small sideways step** into logistics because she avoids big risks.
Reluctance to use AI softens when it's framed as **scouting the threat**.

steps.text: Start a part-time logistics management course within a year
Build the savings cushion to six months of expenses
Try one AI tool for supplier comparisons at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Mateo is 18 and I'm 53. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare, and I'd want it spent well, not wasted on arguments. I'd push the union and the council to write retraining and income support into contracts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel it's mostly manageable for me, but I don't trust the system to use the time. I've seen companies sit on warnings for years. I'd probably do fine, but I'm thinking about the junior buyers like Priya, who'd have the hardest time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd pay the mortgage down and get the cushion up to six months. I'd learn the tools properly, because ten years is enough to be good at them. And I'd start thinking about a role where I'd train or represent others, maybe with the union itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady, with a low hum of concern. It's the one I could plan around, if everyone else plans too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly. What's different about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's time to stop being scared of them. If I have a decade, I can learn one tool a year and see which ones are rubbish. With ten years I could learn the new systems without feeling that my family's mortgage depends on how fast I do it. That pressure is what stops me today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the junior buyers. What would you do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mentor them toward the work that's hardest to automate, the supplier relationships and the dock-side judgement calls. I'd also fight for any retraining budget the company is willing to offer. If I'm senior, I'm in a position to make sure they get something.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to prepare if it isn't wasted on arguments.
I'd push the union to write **retraining** and income support into contracts.
think: I think it's **manageable for me** but I don't trust the system to use the time.
My real concern is the **junior buyers**, who'd have the hardest time.
do: Pay the mortgage down and lift the cushion to **six months**.
Learn the tools properly, about **one tool a year**.
Move toward a **union or training role** later on.
feel: Fairly **steady**, with a low hum of concern about the system.
S4.quote: With ten years I could learn the new systems without feeling that my family's mortgage depends on how fast I do it.
fieldNote: Time **removes her fear** of the tools; the pressure, not the technology, was the barrier.
She turns her seniority into **protection for juniors**, a different stance from her 2028 answer.
She trusts her own plans but not **institutions** to use the decade.

steps.text: Pay the mortgage down and build six months of savings
Learn one new buying tool each year at work
Train towards a mentoring or staff-council role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without question. My whole worry is not having time: no time to retrain, no time to rebuild savings, no time to explain to the kids. What would help is a guaranteed year of income support, paid training that isn't on my evenings, and a say through the union before any tool is rolled out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people in jobs like mine get lumped in with office workers who send emails. Buying is not typing. It's knowing which grower will pick up the phone at five in the morning when the frost comes. I'd want someone to understand that.

headlineQuote: Buying is not typing. It's knowing which grower will pick up the phone at five in the morning when the frost comes.
portrait: Maya Diaz, 43, is **lead buyer** at a fresh-food distributor, with a husband who teaches and two school-age children.
Progressive and union-minded; sits on the **staff council** and distrusts investors more than technology.
Has a **three-month cushion** and a mortgage, so even the calm scenario carries ordinary money worries.
Never uses AI tools; resistance comes from **no paid time** and no proof they handle a late frost.
In the 2028 scenario she expects to **lose her pay** and turns to politics and the union for protection.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, with no time to retrain or rebuild savings.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **year of income support** and paid training that isn't taken from her evenings.
A **union say** before any tool changes the buying team.
